activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

feedback.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+36}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+36}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡1-\operatorname{arsinh}⁡0 \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{{1}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}
$$
